To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the democratic revolutions in the Low Countries were not only the result of a political and ideological struggle between elites, but also of the struggle of ordinary people to gain control over their own lives and to gain a voice in the public sphere.
the Dutch Revolt was not a revolution, that it was a revolt, and that the Revolt is not over yet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the democratic revolution in the sense of the struggle to include all those who are ‘here’ in the political process.
the democratic revolution of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century, and with the question of how it was related to the emergence of modern citizenship.

the question of how the democratic principle of popular sovereignty was interpreted and applied in the revolutionary era, and how the heterogeneity of the people was taken into account in the process of constructing a democracy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
‘We are also (or even more) here’ (Wij zijn er ook, of zelfs meer, nog).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have tried to explore the ‘we’ of democratic revolutions and to show how it was constituted and how it was contested.
we have explored how such differences, and the ways they were addressed and dealt with, shaped the course and outcome of the democratic revolutions in Europe.
it is about the history of democracy, and about the history of the ‘we’.
The main takeaway from our work is that
this is not a problem that is confined to the past.
the history of democracy in the Netherlands, as in other countries, is a history of the inclusion of different groups and the exclusion of others.
the democratic revolutions were also revolutions of citizenship, and that these revolutions were also revolutions for citizenship.
